claim: Yellow ccr2 leaf sectors contained chloroplasts appearing spherical in shape, rather than oval when compared to green leaf tissues from WT or ccr2.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed that yellow ccr2 leaf sectors contained poorly differentiated chloroplasts lacking membrane structures consisting of thylakoid and grana stacks, as well as appearing spherical in shape, rather than oval when compared to green leaf tissues from WT or ccr2 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Chloroplast development can be perturbed in ccr2 leaf primordia cells that develop under extended periods of darkness leading to changes in pigment content.
source: Therefore, chloroplast development can be perturbed in ccr2 leaf primordia cells that develop under extended periods of darkness leading to changes in pigment content.

claim: Green leaf tissues from ccr2 have an altered proportion of β-xanthophylls at the expense of less lutein.

claim: ccr2 plants grown under a longer photoperiod show normal plastid development.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Yellow leaf virescence cannot be attributed to a reduction in lutein, perturbation of SL or ABA biosynthesis.
source: Therefore, we could not attribute yellow leaf virescence to a reduction in lutein, perturbation of SL or ABA biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Both ccr1 and ziso displayed a partial yellow leaf phenotype near the zone of cellular differentiation.
source: Indeed, both ccr1 and ziso displayed a partial yellow leaf phenotype near the zone of cellular differentiation (e.g. petiole-leaf margin), however unlike ccr2 the maturing leaf tissues greened rapidly such that ziso was more similar to WT than ccr2 (Figure 2A).

claim: Unlike ccr2, the maturing leaf tissues of ccr1 and ziso greened rapidly such that ziso was more similar to WT than ccr2.
source: Indeed, both ccr1 and ziso displayed a partial yellow leaf phenotype near the zone of cellular differentiation (e.g. petiole-leaf margin), however unlike ccr2 the maturing leaf tissues greened rapidly such that ziso was more similar to WT than ccr2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Prolonged darkness resulted in notable yellowing of ccr2 leaves and clearly discernible accumulation of tetra-cis-lycopene, neurosporene isomers, ζ-carotene, phytofluene and phytoene.
source: Compared to adult WT leaves, prolonged darkness resulted in notable yellowing of ccr2 leaves and clearly discernible accumulation of tetra-cis-lycopene, neurosporene isomers, ζ-carotene, phytofluene and phytoene (Figure 2B).

claim: The yellow sectors from newly emerged ccr2 leaves accumulated detectable levels of cis-lycopene, neurosporene isomers, ζ-carotene, phytofluene and phytoene after photoperiod shift.

claim: Phytofluene and phytoene were detected in floral buds as well as newly emerged rosette leaves from ccr2, and at trace levels in WT, when plants were grown under a 16 hr photoperiod.
source: Interestingly, even when plants were grown under a 16 hr photoperiod, we could detect phytofluene and phytoene in floral buds as well as newly emerged rosette leaves from ccr2, and at trace levels in WT (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by carotenoid profiling shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A higher ratio of phytofluene and phytoene relative to β-carotene was observed in newly emerged ccr2 tissues, which coincided with a lower percentage of lutein when compared to older tissues.
source: In addition, a higher ratio of phytofluene and phytoene relative to β-carotene was observed in newly emerged ccr2 tissues, which coincided with a lower percentage of lutein when compared to older tissues.
evidence: This is supported by carotenoid profiling data.

claim: Twenty-five revertant lines reproducibly displayed green immature leaves in response to a photoperiod shift.
source: Twenty-five revertant lines reproducibly displayed green immature leaves in response to a photoperiod shift, as exemplified by rccr2−154 and rccr2−155 (Figure 3A).

claim: Leaf tissues of all rccr2 lines contained reduced lutein and xanthophyll composition similar to ccr2.
source: Leaf tissues of all rccr2 lines contained reduced lutein and xanthophyll composition similar to ccr2 (Figure 3B).

claim: When grown under a shorter photoperiod, rccr2 lines produced greener rosettes with less yellow virescence compared to ccr2 and chlorophyll levels were similar to WT.

claim: All rccr2 lines were recessive for the reversion of shorter photoperiod dependent yellow leaves.
source: All rccr2 lines were recessive for the reversion of shorter photoperiod dependent yellow leaves (e.g. rccr2−154 and rccr2−155; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by genetic segregation analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Next generation sequencing identified non-recombinant deserts in chromosome 1 (3605576 bp) and chromosome 4 (6346463 bp) for both rccr2−155 and rccr2−154, respectively.
source: Next generation sequencing (NGS) technologies were used to deep sequence the genomic DNA (gDNA) from leaves of homozygous (M2) plants to identify non-recombinant deserts in chromosome 1 (3605576 bp) and chromosome 4 (6346463 bp) for both rccr2−155 and rccr2−154, respectively (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is supported by NGS mapping data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: Both non-recombinant deserts contained SNPs displaying a discordant chastity value of approximately 1.0 representing the causal mutation of interest.
source: Both non-recombinant deserts contained SNPs displaying a discordant chastity value of approximately 1.0 representing the causal mutation of interest (Austin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by NGS mapping data and a citation to the mapping method.

claim: rccr2−155 lacked recombination at the bottom arm of chromosome one surrounding a single nucleotide polymorphism (G-A mutation at 3606630 bp) within exon 3 of the ZISO gene.

claim: The G-A mutation at 3606630 bp in ZISO caused a premature stop codon leading to a truncated ZISO protein (212 instead of 367 amino acids).
source: This polymorphism caused a premature stop codon leading to a truncated ZISO protein (212 instead of 367 amino acids).
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence analysis.

claim: The overexpression of the functional ZISO cDNA fragment in ccr2 ziso-155 restored ccr2 leaf yellowing in plants grown under an 8 hr photoperiod.
source: The overexpression of the functional ZISO cDNA fragment in ccr2 ziso-155 restored ccr2 leaf yellowing in plants grown under an 8 hr photoperiod (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A double mutant generated by crossing ccr2 with ziso1-4 confirmed the loss-of-function in ziso can restore plastid development in newly emerged immature leaves of ccr2.
source: A double mutant generated by crossing ccr2 with ziso1-4 further confirmed the loss-of-function in ziso can restore plastid development in newly emerged immature leaves of ccr2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Carotenoid analysis of immature leaf tissues of ccr2 ziso-155 revealed reduced lutein and xanthophyll composition similar to ccr2.
source: Carotenoid analysis of immature leaf tissues of ccr2 ziso-155 revealed reduced lutein and xanthophyll composition similar to ccr2, indicating that the complementation of the YL was not due to a change in xanthophyll levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by carotenoid measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The complementation of the YL phenotype in ccr2 ziso-155 was not due to a change in xanthophyll levels.
source: Carotenoid analysis of immature leaf tissues of ccr2 ziso-155 revealed reduced lutein and xanthophyll composition similar to ccr2, indicating that the complementation of the YL was not due to a change in xanthophyll levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the carotenoid analysis.

claim: The epistatic nature between ziso and crtiso revealed that a specific cis-carotene downstream of ZISO activity perturbed plastid development.
source: The epistatic nature between ziso and crtiso revealed that a specific cis-carotene downstream of ZISO activity perturbed plastid development.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic analysis.

claim: ccr2 ziso1-4 had an identical carotenoid profile to that of ziso in that it could only accumulate 9,15,9'-tri-cis-ζ-carotene, phytofluene and phytoene.
source: Analysis of the cis-carotene profile in etiolated cotyledons showed that ccr2 ziso1-4 had an identical carotenoid profile to that of ziso in that it could only accumulate 9,15,9'-tri-cis-ζ-carotene, phytofluene and phytoene (Figure 4C).

claim: ccr2 accumulated lower levels of tri-cis-ζ-carotene, phytofluene and phytoene, yet higher quantities of 9, 9'-di-cis ζ-carotene, 7,9,9'-tri-cis-neurosporene and 7,9,9′,7′-tetra-cis-lycopene, all of which were undetectable in the ziso background.

claim: ziso blocks the biosynthesis of neurosporene isomers, tetra-cis-lycopene and di-cis-ζ-carotene under shorter photoperiods.
source: Therefore, ziso blocks the biosynthesis of neurosporene isomers, tetra-cis-lycopene and di-cis-ζ-carotene under shorter photoperiods, and they themselves or their cleavage products appear to disrupt plastid development in ccr2.
evidence: This is inferred from the carotenoid profiling data.

claim: Neurosporene isomers, tetra-cis-lycopene and di-cis-ζ-carotene or their cleavage products appear to disrupt plastid development in ccr2.
source: Therefore, ziso blocks the biosynthesis of neurosporene isomers, tetra-cis-lycopene and di-cis-ζ-carotene under shorter photoperiods, and they themselves or their cleavage products appear to disrupt plastid development in ccr2.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic and carotenoid profiling data.

claim: 66% of ziso1-4 etioplasts contained PLBs.
source: We observed 66% of ziso1-4 etioplasts contained PLBs (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 4D and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The vast majority (>94%) of etioplasts examined from ccr2 ziso-155 and ccr2 ziso1-4 contained a PLB.
source: Intriguingly, the vast majority (>94%) of etioplasts examined from ccr2 ziso-155 and ccr2 ziso1-4 contained a PLB (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 4D and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Cotyledon greening of de-etiolated seedlings revealed a significant delay in chlorophyll accumulation for both ccr2 and ziso1-4 when compared to WT after 24, 48 and 72 hr of continuous white light.
source: Cotyledon greening of de-etiolated seedlings revealed a significant delay in chlorophyll accumulation for both ccr2 and ziso1-4 when compared to WT after 24, 48 and 72 hr of continuous white light (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by chlorophyll measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cotyledons of the ccr2 ziso-155 and ccr2 ziso1-4 double mutants accumulated levels of chlorophyll similar to that of WT, 48 and 72 hr following de-etiolation.
source: Cotyledons of the ccr2 ziso-155 and ccr2 ziso1-4 double mutants accumulated levels of chlorophyll similar to that of WT, 48 and 72 hr following de-etiolation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by chlorophyll measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A specific cis-carotene produced in ccr2 prevents PLB formation during skotomorphogenesis and perturbs chloroplast development during de-etiolation.
source: We conclude that a specific cis-carotene produced in ccr2 prevents PLB formation during skotomorphogenesis and perturbs chloroplast development during de-etiolation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Compared to WT there were 2- to 4-fold less differentially expressed (DE) genes in ccr2 (ES;191 and JL;1217) than for ccr2 ziso-155 (ES;385 and JL;5550).
source: Compared to WT there were 2- to 4-fold less differentially expressed (DE) genes in ccr2 (ES;191 and JL;1217) than for ccr2 ziso-155 (ES;385 and JL;5550).

claim: Etiolated tissues of ccr2 showed DE genes enriched in photosynthetic processes (17/191; FDR < 3.8xE−06) that were not apparent in ccr2 ziso-155.
source: Etiolated tissues of ccr2 showed DE genes enriched in photosynthetic processes (17/191; FDR < 3.8xE−06) that were not apparent in ccr2 ziso-155, which had DE genes more responsive to a stimulus (134/382; FDR < 3.7xE−7) involving hormones and abiotic stress (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: ccr2 ziso-155 had DE genes more responsive to a stimulus (134/382; FDR < 3.7xE−7) involving hormones and abiotic stress.
source: Etiolated tissues of ccr2 showed DE genes enriched in photosynthetic processes (17/191; FDR < 3.8xE−06) that were not apparent in ccr2 ziso-155, which had DE genes more responsive to a stimulus (134/382; FDR < 3.7xE−7) involving hormones and abiotic stress (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Juvenile leaves of both ccr2 and ccr2 ziso-155 showed a significant enrichment in DE genes responsive to a stimulus involving several hormones and stress.
source: Juvenile leaves of both ccr2 and ccr2 ziso-155 showed a significant enrichment in DE genes also responsive to a stimulus (470/1212; FDR < 2.4xE−34 and 1724/5510; FDR < 5.4xE−43, respectively) involving several hormones and stress.
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: DE genes specific to ccr2 ziso-155 juvenile leaves were involved in biological regulation (1623/5510; FDR < 4.2xE−30) and epigenetic processes (184/5510; FDR < 3.1xE−11) such as DNA methylation, histone modification and gene silencing.
source: Even more intriguing was the enhanced enrichment of DE genes specific to ccr2 ziso-155 juvenile leaves that were involved in biological regulation (1623/5510; FDR < 4.2xE−30) and epigenetic processes (184/5510; FDR < 3.1xE−11) such as DNA methylation, histone modification and gene silencing (Supplementary file 4).

claim: Norflurazon induced 30–35% of DE genes in ccr2, which was not apparent in ccr2 ziso-155 (12–14%).

claim: Etiolated seedlings of ccr2 and NF treated de-etiolated seedlings shared a 15–21% overlap in DE genes.

evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis with published data.

claim: There was no clear overlap in DE genes associated with a brief period of white light following de-etiolation under far red light that induced generation of singlet oxygen.

evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis with published data.

claim: DE genes in ccr2 shared 31–42% in common with the cop9 and cop1 mutants.
source: An unexpected finding was the DE genes in ccr2 shared 31–42% in common with the cop9 and cop1 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis using Genevestigator.

claim: ccr2 ziso-155 contra-regulated the DE genes in cop9, but not those in cop1.
source: ccr2 ziso-155 contra-regulated the DE genes in cop9, but not those in cop1.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis using Genevestigator.

claim: Genes regulated during light-mediated germination were contra-expressed in ccr2 (28–48%), yet co-expressed in ccr2 ziso-155 (44–48%).
source: Genes regulated during light-mediated germination were contra-expressed in ccr2 (28–48%), yet co-expressed in ccr2 ziso-155 (44–48%).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis using Genevestigator.

claim: None of the 20 contra-regulated genes were miss-regulated by a brief period of white light following de-etiolation under far red light treatment.

claim: A lower PIF3/HY5 ratio can be associated with PhANG expression.
source: A lower PIF3/HY5 ratio can be associated with PhANG expression.

source: This would lead to a lower PIF3/HY5 ratio in ccr2 ziso-155 when compared to WT.

evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis.

claim: ccr2 regulates a unique set of genes not related to a NF generated or GUN5 mediated retrograde signal.
source: This highlights that ccr2 regulates a unique set of genes not related to a NF generated or GUN5 mediated retrograde signal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis.

source: In summary, the repression of negative regulators of photomorphogenesis, correlates well with the up-regulation of PhANG expression in ccr2 ziso-155 and links cis-carotene accumulation to the regulation of a unique gene set involved in mediating plastid development.

claim: The repression of negative regulators of photomorphogenesis links cis-carotene accumulation to the regulation of a unique gene set involved in mediating plastid development.

claim: The normal DET1 transcript (which contains exon 4) was repressed in ccr2 det1-154.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis confirmed that the shorter DET1-154 transcript (spliced and missing exon 4) was highly enriched (approx. 200 fold) in ccr2 det1-154, while the normal DET1 transcript (which contains exon 4) was repressed in ccr2 det1-154 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

source: The phenotypes of ccr2 det1-154 and det1-154 were intermediate to that of det1-1 (Chory et al., 1989), showing a smaller rosette with a shorter floral stem height and reduced fertility relative to the WT (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The xanthophylls and β-carotene were all significantly reduced by det1-154.

claim: di-cis-ζ-carotene, pro-neurosporene and tetra-cis-lycopene were significantly reduced in ccr2 det1-154.

claim: D15 significantly enhanced di-cis-ζ-carotene and pro-neurosporene, yet reduced tetra-cis-lycopene in etiolated cotyledons of ccr2.

evidence: This is supported by carotenoid profiling shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In WT etiolated cotyledons, D15 significantly enhanced violaxanthin, neoxanthin and antheraxanthin content.

claim: Treatment of dark and light grown wild type seedlings with D15 did not cause adverse pleiotropic effects on cotyledon greening, hypocotyl elongation or plastid development in cotyledons.

claim: Apocarotenoid formation from either cleavage of di-cis-ζ-carotene and/or pro-neurosporene in ccr2 can perturb PLB formation independent of PChlide biosynthesis.

claim: The ccr2 generated cis-carotene cleavage product can override the negative regulation of PORA transcription enabled by det1-154, yet does not alter PORA expression when compared to WT.

source: Therefore, cis-carotene cleavage in ccr2 generated a signal that can block det1-154 mediated repression of PORA transcription and restore WT POR protein levels and PLB formation in det1-154.

source: The PIF3 and HY5 mRNA expression levels were not significantly different in det1-154 compared to WT, regardless of D15 treatment.

evidence: This is supported by western blot data.

source: LHCB2 mRNA and protein expression was significantly reduced in ccr2, and was restored back to WT expression levels by D15 treatment (Figure 8C).

source: The reduction in LHCB2 gene expression was consistent with our transcriptomic analysis in virescent leaf tissues of ccr2 (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Table 2.

claim: A ccr2 generated cis-carotene cleavage product can transcriptionally enhance the PIF3/HY5 ratio during photomorphogenesis thereby reducing PhANG expression and greening of ccr2 seedlings.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and illustrated in Figure 8D.

source: We attribute ccr2 leaf viresence to the fine-tuning of plastid development in leaf primordia cells as a consequence of cis-carotene accumulation and not the generation of singlet oxygen (Kato et al., 2009; Chai et al., 2011; Han et al., 2012; Page et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and citations to previous research.

source: Our evidence revealed that leaf virescence was linked to the hyper-accumulation of specific cis-carotenes since, ziso-155 and det1-154 as well as D15 were able to reduce cis-carotene biosynthesis in ccr2 tissues, andrestore leaf greening in plants grown under a shorter photoperiod (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: This is in agreement with evidence showing cis-carotenes are cleavable in vitro by CCD7 enzymatic activity.

claim: CCD4 activity is necessary for generation of a cis-carotene derived apocarotenoid signal in zds/clb5, which affected leaf development.
source: This is in agreement with evidence showing cis-carotenes are cleavable in vitro by CCD7 enzymatic activity (Bruno et al., 2016) and that CCD4 activity is necessary for generation of a cis-carotene derived apocarotenoid signal in zds/clb5, which affected leaf development (Avendaño-Vázquez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The apocarotenoid signal and DET1 regulate an unknown factor necessary for PLB formation that is independent of POR abundance and GUN activity.
source: As an alternative hypothesis we propose that the apocarotenoid signal and DET1 regulate an unknown factor necessary for PLB formation that is independent of POR abundance and GUN activity (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental observations and illustrated in Figure 7E.

claim: The ccr2-generated apocarotenoid acted in a retrograde manner to transcriptionally regulate POR, PIF3 and HY5 transcript levels in ccr2 and ccr2 det1-154 backgrounds.
source: Here we demonstrate that the ccr2-generated apocarotenoid acted in a retrograde manner to transcriptionally regulate POR, PIF3 and HY5 transcript levels in ccr2 and ccr2 det1-154 backgrounds (Figures 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The abundances of POR, PIF3 and HY5 transcript and protein levels were reverted in ccr2 det1-154 to expected levels for det1 mutants by treatment with D15.
source: Of particular interest is how the abundances of all three transcript and protein levels were reverted in ccr2 det1-154 to expected levels for det1 mutants by treatment with D15.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data.

claim: D15 reverted HY5 and PIF3 transcript and protein levels back to WT levels in ccr2.
source: Similarly, D15 reverted HY5 and PIF3 transcript and protein levels back to WT levels in ccr2.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data.

claim: The contra-regulation of the PIF3/HY5 ratio by D15 treatment was further contrasted by an even lower PIF3/HY5 ratio in the ccr2 ziso-155 mutant etiolated seedlings and leaves collected from plants grown under a shorter photoperiod.
source: The contra-regulation of the PIF3/HY5 ratio by D15 treatment was further contrasted by an even lower PIF3/HY5 ratio (due to the up-regulation of HY5 and reduction in PIF3 transcript levels compared to WT) in the ccr2 ziso-155 mutant etiolated seedlings and leaves collected from plants grown under a shorter photoperiod (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Table 2.

claim: The loss-of-function in ZISO can block substrate production in the dark and limit biosynthesis of tri-cis-ζ-carotene and neurosporene in leaves from ccr2 ziso-155 plants grown under a shorter photoperiod when photoisomerisation becomes rate-limited.
source: While D15 has been shown to only impair substrate cleavage, the loss-of-function in ZISO can block substrate production in the dark (Figure 4) and limit biosynthesis of tri-cis-ζ-carotene and neurosporene in leaves from ccr2 ziso-155 plants grown under a shorter photoperiod when photoisomerisation becomes rate-limited.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Under favourable conditions of light, when activity of ZISO, CRTISO as well as photoisomerisation are not limited, the absence of the cis-carotene derived cleavage product enables the lowering of the PIF3/HY5 ratio to maintain PhANG expression in concert with chloroplast development.
source: Under favourable conditions of light, when activity of ZISO, CRTISO as well as photoisomerisation are not limited, the absence of the cis-carotene derived cleavage product enables the lowering of the PIF3/HY5 ratio to maintain PhANG expression in concert with chloroplast development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: cis-carotenes will hyper-accumulate in etiolated cotyledons and younger leaf tissues exposed to an extended dark period when CRTISO activity becomes rate-limited, such as in the absence of chromatin-modifying enzyme, SDG8.
source: cis-carotenes will hyper-accumulate in etiolated cotyledons and younger leaf tissues exposed to an extended dark period when CRTISO activity becomes rate-limited, such as in the absence of chromatin-modifying enzyme, SDG8.
evidence: This is a statement about the conditions under which cis-carotenes accumulate.

claim: SDG8 is required for permissive expression of CRTISO in developing seedlings and shoot meristem.
source: SDG8 is required for permissive expression of CRTISO in developing seedlings and shoot meristem (Cazzonelli et al., 2009b; Cazzonelli et al., 2009a; Cazzonelli et al., 2010) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: SDG8 transcript levels are developmentally regulated, increasing from low basal levels after germination and declining during the dark phase of the diurnal cycle.
source: SDG8 transcript levels are developmentally regulated, increasing from low basal levels after germination and declining during the dark phase of the diurnal cycle (Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A perturbation in cis-carotene accumulation in ccr2 ziso-155 juvenile leaves grown under a shorter photoperiod is linked to an enriched gene ontology in chromatin and DNA modifying processes, in particularly the repression of DET1 gene expression.
source: Here we linked a perturbation in cis-carotene accumulation in ccr2 ziso-155 juvenile leaves grown under a shorter photoperiod to an enriched gene ontology in chromatin and DNA modifying processes, in particularly the repression of DET1 gene expression (Supplementary file 4 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: DET1 was required for cis-carotene biosynthesis in wild type tissues, as det1 mutants accumulate phytoene, phytofluene and tri-cis-ζ-carotene.
source: DET1 was required for cis-carotene biosynthesis in wild type tissues, as det1 mutants accumulate phytoene, phytofluene and tri-cis-ζ-carotene (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by carotenoid profiling shown in Supplementary file 6.

claim: The down-regulation and/or loss-of-function in det1 in tomato lines revealed an accumulation of phytoene and phytofluene in ripe fruits.
source: Similarly, the down-regulation and/or loss-of-function in det1 in tomato lines revealed an accumulation of phytoene and phytofluene in ripe fruits (Enfissi et al., 2010; Talens et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CRTISO and DET1 can control the accumulation of cis-carotenes and the apocarotenoid signal that regulates plastid development, a process that perhaps is fine-tuned with epigenetic and chromatin modifying processes that control light-mediated development.
source: Therefore, CRTISO and DET1 can control the accumulation of cis-carotenes and the apocarotenoid signal that regulates plastid development, a process that perhaps is fine-tuned with epigenetic and chromatin modifying processes that control light-mediated development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: ccr2 and det1 oppositely regulate the chlorophyll biosynthetic enzyme, POR at the transcriptional level during skotomorphogenesis.
source: Herein we revealed how ccr2 and det1 oppositely regulate the chlorophyll biosynthetic enzyme, POR at the transcriptional level during skotomorphogenesis (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 7.

claim: There are relatively few mutants published to date that do not produce a PLB in dark grown tissues and all, except ccr2, are due to reduced levels of PORA and/or PChlide.
source: There are relatively few mutants published to date that do not produce a PLB in dark grown tissues and all, except ccr2, are due to reduced levels of PORA and/or PChlide.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Arabidopsis mutants like det1-1 and cop1 mutants have less photoactive PChlide-F655 and higher total PChlide levels due to a reduction in POR that thereby blocks PLB formation.
source: Arabidopsis mutants like det1-1 and cop1 mutants have less photoactive PChlide-F655 and higher total PChlide levels due to a reduction in POR that thereby blocks PLB formation (Sperling et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Like det1-1, det1-154 exhibits all the same phenotypes and indeed D15 treatment of ccr2 det1-154 blocked PLB formation.
source: Like det1-1, det1-154 exhibits all the same phenotypes and indeed D15 treatment of ccr2 det1-154 blocked PLB formation (Chory et al., 1989) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Table 1, and a citation to previous research.

claim: While etioplasts in ccr2 dark grown cotyledons do not make a PLB, the abundance of POR and PChlide levels are similar to wild type.
source: While etioplasts in ccr2 dark grown cotyledons do not make a PLB, the abundance of POR and PChlide levels are similar to wild type (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: ccr2 and det1 control PLB formation via distinct, although perhaps mutually dependent signalling pathways, whereby the cis-carotene derived signal blocks the det1-mediated transcriptional repression of PORA gene expression.
source: Therefore, ccr2 and det1 control PLB formation via distinct, although perhaps mutually dependent signalling pathways, whereby the cis-carotene derived signal blocks the det1-mediated transcriptional repression of PORA gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: ccr2 and ccr2 ziso-155 displayed closed cotyledons, an apical hook and normal hypocotyl length revealing that the cis-carotene derived cleavage metabolite does not activate photomorphogenesis.
source: First, ccr2 and ccr2 ziso-155 displayed closed cotyledons, an apical hook and normal hypocotyl length revealing that the cis-carotene derived cleavage metabolite does not activate photomorphogenesis (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Table 1.

claim: DET1 protein levels were relatively unchanged in WT, ccr2, det1-154 and ccr2 det1-154, regardless of D15 chemical inhibition.
source: Second, DET1 protein levels were relatively unchanged in WT, ccr2, det1-154 and ccr2 det1-154, regardless of D15 chemical inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data.

claim: The cis-carotene-derived apocarotenoid cleavage product can transcriptionally up-regulate POR levels in det1, thereby enabling PLB formation in etioplasts and chloroplast differentiation following de-etiolation.
source: Hence, the cis-carotene-derived apocarotenoid cleavage product can transcriptionally up-regulate POR levels in det1, thereby enabling PLB formation in etioplasts and chloroplast differentiation following de-etiolation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: DET1 encodes a nuclear protein acting downstream from the phytochrome photoreceptors to negatively regulate light-driven seedling development and promote skotomorphogenesis.
source: DET1 encodes a nuclear protein acting downstream from the phytochrome photoreceptors to negatively regulate light-driven seedling development and promote skotomorphogenesis (Schroeder et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: DET1 interacts with COP1 and the chromatin regulator DDB1, to limit the access of transcription factors to promoters and negatively regulate the expression of hundreds of genes via chromatin interactions.
source: DET1 interacts with COP1 and the chromatin regulator DDB1, to limit the access of transcription factors to promoters and negatively regulate the expression of hundreds of genes via chromatin interactions (Schroeder et al., 2002; Lau and Deng, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Light stimulates photomorphogenesis and the rapid down-regulation of DET1 leading to a lower PIF3/HY5 protein ratio and the up-regulation of PhANG expression according to published results.
source: Light stimulates photomorphogenesis and the rapid down-regulation of DET1 leading to a lower PIF3/HY5 protein ratio and the up-regulation of PhANG expression according to published results.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge from published research.

claim: Genetic mutations in cop1 and det1 also lower the PIF3/HY5 ratio and activate PhANG expression.
source: Genetic mutations in cop1 and det1 also lower the PIF3/HY5 ratio and activate PhANG expression (Osterlund et al., 2000; Benvenuto et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ccr2 det1-154 etiolated and de-etiolated seedlings treated with D15 displayed higher HY5 and lower PIF3 protein levels, contrasting opposite to that of ccr2.
source: Consistent with these findings, ccr2 det1-154 etiolated and de-etiolated seedlings treated with D15 displayed higher HY5 and lower PIF3 protein levels, contrasting opposite to that of ccr2 (Figures 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The cis-carotene derived cleavage metabolite can transcriptionally antagonise the DET1 mediated post-transcriptional regulation of HY5 and PIF3.
source: The cis-carotene derived cleavage metabolite can transcriptionally antagonise the DET1 mediated post-transcriptional regulation of HY5 and PIF3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The unknown apocarotenoid retrograde signal acts at the transcriptional level in parallel with the negative regulator DET1, to control POR, PIF3 and HY5 and thus regulate etioplast development during skotomorphogenesis and chloroplast development under extended periods of darkness.
source: In conclusion, we deduce that the unknown apocarotenoid retrograde signal acts at the transcriptional level in parallel with the negative regulator DET1, to control POR, PIF3 and HY5 and thus regulate etioplast development during skotomorphogenesis and chloroplast development under extended periods of darkness (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and illustrated in Figure 9.
